Ba2+ induces long-duration, voltage-independent “action potentials” in osteoblastic ROS cells by a process that is blocked by L-type Ca2+-channel blockers.
Ba2+ can induce action potentials in ROS 17/2 cells by opening L-type Ca2+.

In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of calcium in the regulation of cell function.
the role of Ca2+ and Ca2+-related second messengers in bone formation and bone cell differentiation.
the effects of Ba2+ on the L-type Ca2+, and the L-type Ca+ channels.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
Ba2+ is a potent activator of L-type Ca channels in osteoblastic ROS 17/2,8 cells.
Ba2+ can open L-type Ca2+, and that this opening is not inhibited by TTX.
the Ba2+-induced pulses are due to the opening of L-type channels in the absence of voltage, and that the pulses are not action potentials.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
Ba2+ induces L-type Ca2+-channel openings that result in action potentials in osteocytic cells.
Ba2+ is able to induce action potential-like currents and voltages in ROS 17/2 cells.
Ba2+ is a “physiological” activator of L-type Ca channels in osteoblasts.
The main takeaway from our work is that
Ba2+ is not an innocent bystander in studies of voltage-gated Ca2+ channels.
L-type Ca2+-channel blockers can be used to study the effects of Ca2+ influx in osteoblasts.
Ba2+, a non-physiological cation, can be used to induce L-type Ca2+, voltage-dependent, channels to open in the absence of membrane potential change.
